utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber was informed that the Prosecution had a preliminary to be raised. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Thank you. Your Honours, this is with respect to two exhibits, P409, it is an admitted exhibit, but it lacks an English translation. One is available and has been uploaded, and the Prosecution would request that the registrar be authorised to attach it. The second matter is P459. If Your Honours will recall, that was the document admitted yesterday upon which the translation had unrevised copy blocking some words. The Prosecution has now uploaded a clean copy and that is available -- or we are requesting that it replace the current version in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groome. Mr. Lukic, I take it that the Defence will have had an opportunity to look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honour, I was submerged into this and the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you agree that since it's just --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- translations that we would grant leave to have them added.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then if there's any problem, then we'd like to hear from you soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Madam Registrar, leave is hereby granted to attach to Exhibit 409 the English translation as uploaded into e-court by the Prosecution and to replace the translation attached to P459, English translation by the new translation uploaded by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, and then just to -- to make the Chamber aware that the way witnesses -- the witness schedule is working out this week, it looks like the - at least according to Prosecution's calculations - that the witness that will be called Friday may need to go into next week. I'm not sure of that. But I do want to just alert the Chamber to the fact that next week is a rather full week and a rather complicated week because of the need to get Danish interpreters and that, so it may be that the Prosecution next Monday might be asking the Chamber to investigate the possibility of sitting an extra hour to accommodate some exigencies which I can explain at that time, but I just wanted to alert the Chamber at this time as to that. Your Honour, then there's another matter. Next week, the witness -- first witness of the week, we will be using military maps, and they are maps 40, 41, and 48 in the Sarajevo Court binder. Your Honour, these maps, they're very difficult to comprehend at the size they are in the Court binder. The Prosecution has had them reproduced in their original size and they are quite large, but they are a very important piece of evidence. The Prosecution also believes that it is only fair that Mr. Mladic have an opportunity to see the maps and discuss them with his attorneys, so the Prosecution was proposing or seeking the permission of the court to line them up against this back wall where they could not be seen from the public gallery sometime today so that Mr. Mladic can view them with his attorney. It will also give us an opportunity to work with the director and to come up with some strategy for making them available in a useable way for the Chamber and for the public. So I'm requesting to put three maps at the back of the courtroom today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, thank you for the forewarning about scheduling for next week. Second, the maps may be put against the wall so that Mr. Mladic has an opportunity to look at them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And finally, Your Honour, for this morning, I made a proposal yesterday, and it would be appreciated if we could hear the Defence views on it, we have prepared the materials to provide CLSS if the proposal is adopted, but I will not do -- obviously not do that until there's a decision by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, are you in a position yet to respond to the request and suggestion made by Mr. Groome yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid I was reading. Can -- can I -- what's the proposal from yesterday?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The proposal from yesterday was about the way how to prepare for the -- for the recognition of voices it was, isn't it, Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, on tape-recorded intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, we agree with that proposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You agree with the proposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber also agrees that you proceed as you suggested and requested.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nothing else. If there's nothing else, could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Philipps.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given yesterday at the beginning of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic will now continue his cross-examination. Mr. Lukic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Philipps. When we broke off yesterday, I put a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in order to continue, could we have 1D419, please, on our screens. We need page 3. From line 11 until the end of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We talked about operational groups, tactical groups, and about the units that made them up. In line 11 and further on, in the Galic trial, the date is the 16th of July, 2002, there is what you say: [In English] "As I understand it, these [sic] brigades or parts of those brigades formed part of the operational tactical group at various times. It may be that at one moment all of them were part of it or it may be at other times that only some of them or part of each brigade was within the tactical Operational Group."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sorry for interrupting for a moment. Can that be enlarged, please, from line 11 on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And then you continue at line 23 at the end of this row: "The group was brought together for specific purposes and may have used all the brigade or may have used parts of the brigades." [Interpretation] May we conclude that your chart does not show which brigades and possibly which parts of certain brigades took part in the operations for which these operational or tactical groups were organised?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now we need page 8 of this document. Lines 13 through 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The question was as follows: "Mr. Philipps, [in English] to conclude that the Ilidza Brigade and the Igman Brigade in the period of 1993 -- that is, from this report, could we conclude that the Ilijas and the Igman Brigade were not part of the Vogosca Tactical Group? Ilidza Brigade and Igman brigade." And your answer at line 17 was, I quote: "Yes, that would be a conclusion from this document on that date." [Interpretation] Do you stand by this answer today as well?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is the -- is the reference the document referring to the chart that was presented during the Galic case?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that's a -- we don't have that document in front of us. But so from memory, I'm unable to confirm what was on the Galic chart of the SRK. It's very similar to the two charts we have here today but may be subtly different in some way without me saying it. But generally speaking, we seem to have established that the Vogosca Operational Group or the Vogosca Tactical Group had different brigades in it at different times, and I don't have the documents that show which brigades were in it and when they seem to be moving in and out, depending on the tactical operational situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Harbour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: The Defence says that this answer refers to the chart that Mr. Philipps produced in the Galic case. However, if we look on page 7 of the excerpt of the Galic testimony, it appears that the answer refers to an SRK report that was put to the witness during that case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I think Mr. Philipps showed awareness that apparently a document played a role in this discussion and he doesn't know which document which exactly that was. Now, I think the best way to proceed would at least be to give access to that document to Mr. Philipps, because it might be difficult for him to work from the top of his head.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I can rephrase the question so we -- because I don't have that document in the system. We can use this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it visible from the document we are using in this case; that is, the chart for 1999 [sic] to 1994. Is it the same conclusion that can you draw from that document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you say the chart from 1994?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This -- the chart that is --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What did I say?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You said 1999 to 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Thank you, Your Honour. 1992 to 1994.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In -- to answer your question, on the chart 1992 to 1994, four brigades are shown with a faint but solid line as being part of Vogosca operational or tactical group. That is the Ilidza, Ilijas, Rajlovac and Vogosca Infantry Brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that something changed now in relation to the previous situation; namely, that the Ilidza Brigade is part of this group?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only refer to all the documents that I used to reach this conclusion of which there were one, two, three, four, five separate documents, all of which covered the composition of Vogosca Operational/Tactical Group. That includes an order by Colonel Marcetic about the forming of the tactical group in 1993, where we had the discussion whether that was June or July.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now I'd like to ask you the following. In which way was there co-operation between the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and how did they communicate, actually, with the brigade command? I beg your pardon. If, for example, fire was needed from artillery weapons --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all unnecessary microphones please be switched off. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you give us an answer?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I was -- I hadn't understood the end of the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Maybe it was inartfully posed. How would corps and brigade commands or staffs co-operate if the use of artillery was asked for?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand. There was several means of communication between the corps commander and the brigade commander, brigade commanders. This could be done in person, verbally, where they were co-located, and during meeting where the corps commander could talk in person to the brigade commander, but this would be a rare event. Mostly a brigade commander would be communicated to either by runner or by field telephone or by radio. The disadvantage of the latter is that, of course, it can be intercepted, and the disadvantage of a runner and a field telephone is that they can both be intercepted by enemy fire. Intercepted in the sense of destroyed in the latter case. To call in artillery fire usually requires radio, that's because it's required immediately in a certain position. As many of the artillery locations were fixed through the period, many were laid with field telephone, I imagine, is what you would do if you had fixed artillery. And so either land-lines or radio could be used to call in artillery fire. And at that time in Sarajevo I suspect that maybe the telephone system would partially work within a city, so there might even be a method which we don't normally expect in warfare of being able to use the simple telecommunications system by dialing a telephone number.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. That's as far as the technical side of this communication is concerned. Do you know, though, which persons are communicating in order to have fire support? Both from the corps and from the brigade.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In -- in such a case obviously the corps and brigade commanders themselves are not involved. The corps commander or the brigade commanders might require the fire to be brought in, in a particular place, but they would have staffs that would actually do the communication for them rather than make the calls themselves. Occasionally a corps commander or a brigade commander might talk personally to an artillery commander to bring in the appropriate fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So could this communication take place apart from the commanders? Could representatives of staffs communicate directly?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a sense now we're outside the scope of my knowledge. I know how it works in other armies, I know how it ought to work in certain organisations, but how it actually functioned within the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps is something that I have not looked at. I would be very surprised if the staff didn't communicate with the staff in -- in the brigade headquarters. So Corps Staff and brigade staff would talk to each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But you don't know for sure.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic is kindly asked to wait for the B/C/S translation to be over before putting his next question in B/C/S because otherwise we are overlapping and a part of the witness's answer is lost.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you're reading your screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [B/C/S on English channel]... about military post 7491, and you said that that was a paramilitary formation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Military post 7491, as far as I know, is the Ilijas Infantry Brigade, and I don't believe Ilijas Brigade --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where we are in our chart?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Vasko's Platoon -- sorry. Do you remember that you mentioned that platoon, Vasko's Platoon, and that you determined that it was a paramilitary formation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I located a platoon called Vasko's Platoon with a VP number of 7491/20, and the 7491 prefix indicated that it was part of the Ilijas Brigade. And then I used two documents to establish this: A daily combat report of November 1993 and information on the transfer of soldiers within the Ilijas Brigade in December 1993. And I have the ERNs if that would assist the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I only ask that if the Defence is referring to something that the witness said in his prior testimony, that that just be made clear for the record since this information wasn't elicited from the witness in this case yet. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That seems like a good suggestion, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Since the witness knows what I'm talking about, I'll just put the follow-up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But we would like to know what you are talking about as well. So if there's any reference to earlier testimony --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't have reference here, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we'll see. And the date again was, mister ... the date of the testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't have the reference at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nothing at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then we --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But I can pose a general question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Philipps, if a formation were to have a VP number and if it were to be included in the system of command and control, would it then be a paramilitary formation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: To answer that, generally speaking I would not expect that to be a paramilitary organisation. And I don't think, in fact I'm sure on both of these charts where Vasko's platoon is shown, and in my alphanumeric listing, no mention is made of it being a paramilitary formation. Paramilitary is a very emotive term and is often misunderstood and it's not often a term I would use. If I used it in the Galic case, I would be pleased to see the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You heard me that I don't have that reference and we move on.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that -- even the date when the witness testified in Galic, is that not known?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's 16th and 17th of July, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 16th and 17th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. We could have a look at it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to ask you something about artillery pieces now within the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. On page 11745 -- the document is 1D419. In this document, it is page 11. And it is the 16th of July, 2002. Again, it is the transcript from the Galic trial. We see here that there were howitzers in a mixed artillery division. Lines 10 through 16 in this transcript. You say that this particular artillery piece was involved with Colonel Jovo Bartula "[In English]... and the relationship, therefore, between the battery and the commander at that period has been used to identify those batteries." [Interpretation] May we agree that howitzers are not anti-armour weapons?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that howitzers are not anti-armour weapons. They have a capability against armour but are not generally used against armoured equipment. A good example would, of course, would be the 122-millimetre howitzer that does have an anti-tank shell that can be used for direct anti-tank fire that was in use by the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Howitzers are not normally found in such anti-armour units; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. It would be an odd thing to find a howitzer in an anti-tank artillery regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Within this mixed anti-armour artillery regiment, you have shown three batteries, and they are all connected with dotted lines.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're referring to both the charts, I see that the 4th Mixed Anti-Tank Artillery Regiment has no subordinated equipment, whereas the mixed artillery regiment on the bottom left of the chart has multiple batteries associated with firing positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This dotted line indicates that you were unable to confirm this with certainty, where it belonged.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. This data came from a very detailed fire planning map, which was drawn up by the 4th Mixed Artillery Regiment showing positions of weapons at four different locations, as well as the fire plan that they would undertake in the event of an operation. And the conclusion is that since the 4th Mixed Artillery Regiment drew up the fire plan for the under-listed artillery pieces, that those artillery pieces were part of the 4th Mixed Artillery Regiment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, if you allow me to interrupt. Galic transcript, page 11.774, 17th of July, seems to deal with paramilitary formations, although not necessarily and immediately in relation to a named unit. And I wonder if can I find it in two minutes, Mr. Lukic, whether one of the members of your staff could not find the same in two minutes, if we've got the dates of the transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your help, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Harbour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Just for clarification, and if it assists the Defence, the witness testified on four days in the Galic case. The 5th, 10th, 16th, and 17th of July, 2002.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I looked only at the 16th and the 17th at this moment because these were the dates given. And the page -- yes, I gave the page reference already. Perhaps your team could look at the other dates whether any reference to paramilitary formations is there. If you would not mind, I'll read to the witness what he said in relation to paramilitary formations where Judge El Mahdi asked him the following: "Did you find out about the relationship, if any, between the corps and paramilitary forces? The answer then was: "The existence of paramilitary formations, to use that term, is shown on the chart with the one example of a unit that I could not link directly to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. And that is shown on the right-hand side of the chart. Other organisations which had been termed 'paramilitary' were later shown or may have been incorporated within the corps itself, that is, were no longer paramilitary, that is outside the military, but were brought into the military and under the command of the corps." And then there's a further explanation about that one example. This is, I think, the relevant part. So if you would like to give it some follow-up or if the witness, on the basis of what I just read to him, and it's -- again, it's not the entire answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That passage I would, in a sense, give exactly the same wording again if I could be so eloquent now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I hope you didn't lose too much of your eloquence over the years, Mr. Philipps. But please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Philipps, let us now focus on the personnel composition of the SRK and by naming some names we're going to do that. Let's start with Tomislav Sipcic. He was the first commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: On my charts, he is the first commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps during the period.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Have you established when was it that he assumed his duties?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters are kindly asking Mr. Lukic to wait for the B/C/S translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, a renewed request for you on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On my chart, based on a very limited number of documents, I have Tomislav Sipcic as being in post in July 1992 but possibly in post before that date, and in post in August 1992 and possibly in post after that date. But I do not have the exact dates of his appointment and the exact dates of his relinquishment of command. Later we find documents with his name but not his signature, and it may be that he relinquished command but his name was still being used.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us look at document 03698. That's a 65 ter document. Mr. Philipps, as we can see this document is from May 1992. And let us look at the last page of this document. So it's a document sent from the SRK command, and we can see the signature of Tomislav Sipcic. Would you agree with me that Mr. Sipcic was at the head of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps in May 1992, i.e., before June 1992?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can agree that I can see the name of Tomislav Sipcic. I don't see a signature. But it being a military communication, I wouldn't necessarily have expected a signature. And, however, I also agree with you that if the document is dated May 1992, then the chart could be amended to say May 1992 but would still have the dash before it because all we've done is extend the date at which we believe he is the commander. He may have been posted to that position earlier. If I'd had this document it could have been added to the chart and that date amended by one month.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: By looking at this document, would you agree that this is the format of a dispatch?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because of the typeface and the way that the document is typed and the look of it. It looks like a document typed for communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Such documents were never signed, in fact; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very rare for them to be signed. Very rare.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your work, did you come across information that Tomislav Sipcic had left the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and that Stanislav Galic had not assumed the position of the corps commander and that, at that time, the only one who carried out any command duties was Cedo Sladoje?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will have to break that question down into parts. I came across documents that showed when Stanislav Galic became the corps commander relating to a meeting that took place in Jahorina in September 1992. I did not find a document removing Tomislav Sipcic from command, but his name continued to appear on documents up to September 1992, but none of them were signed. On my chart I show a dotted line between Tomislav Sipcic and the hand-over to Stanislav Galic, and so it is quite possible that a subordinate took over command of the corps in the absence of the corps commander, as we discussed yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now I'm interested in the name of Veljko Stojanovic. He was in the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised, or motorised, Brigade from May 1992 until 1996. However, at the same time, in your chart, Mr. Veljko Stojanovic is designated as the deputy commander in the 1st Infantry Brigade from --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Lukic please repeat the dates slowly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you're invited to slowly repeat the dates you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So, in your chart, Mr. Veljko Stojanovic is designated as the brigade deputy commander in the 1st Romanija Infantry Brigade from the 12th September 1992 until 10th January 1993. My question is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we look at where we are in the chart because I think earlier you said mechanized or motorised brigade and now you are referring to the infantry brigade. Is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 1st Romanija Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Then we, I think -- yes, you said something different in page 18, line 1 and 2. But now let's try and find ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that, indeed, in your chart this person is occupying two posts and covering the same period?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Being based on documentary information, I have multiple documents relating to Veljko Stojanovic as the deputy brigade commander of -- of one organisation and as the brigade commander of another organisation. I have, if you look at my alphabetical list, listed Veljko Stojanovic twice, once with a prefix number 2 around his name. It is impossible for me to conclude that these individuals are the same person without direct proof that they are the same person. It is perfectly possible with my documentation that Veljko Stojanovic was the name of two people. I think it unlikely that they're two people, but if I -- if I make conclusions that aren't based on documents, then I'm leaping to conclusions and that -- that causes enormous difficulties. That is why his name appears twice on the chart and appears twice in the alphabetical list. In reality, if we were to go through the documents in detail, we might find that he occupied one position for a period of time, then occupied another position, and then returned to his original brigade. I can only think of examples where other officers in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps have moved from one brigade and one post to another and their name will appear several times on the chart, and they can often be shown to be the same person. In this case I have been unable to prove that it's the same person, and so his name appears twice in the alphabetical list.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If it is the same person, that person could not have discharged both duties simultaneously, at the same time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be correct. You could not be the brigade commander of one brigade and the -- and the deputy commander of another brigade at the same time. So the logical conclusion would that be it's one person that's had two different posts, but without a document where I can conclusively say they are the same person, then I can't join these two sets together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one thing in this context. For Veljko Stojanovic, in his position as deputy brigade commander, there's no indication whatsoever about the time. May I take it that from the documents -- well, at least there must be some kind of a time indication?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If I look at the -- the entry for the documents relating to his post as deputy brigade commander, I can see that the documents do have dates, and it would be possible to look at those documents and extract the dates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because nothing of the kind is found on the chart.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whereas for his position as brigade commander, there are -- there's a rather wide time range, May 1992 until December 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 1996, I think it says on the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me see. Let me see. I have to enlarge that. Yes, but I'm looking at the chart at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me see. Let me see whether I can find that. I find on the chart for the 1st Sarajevo Mechanized, or motorised, Brigade, Stojanovic, Veljko, May 1992 up to December 1995, and then again a dash, which means that it could be for later, but -- yes. I've enlarged it on my screen in such a way that even one of my colleagues confirms.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's different in the Veljko Stojanovic, 2, as a brigade commander, where it says 1992 to 1996.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I have -- I now need... oh. Are there various versions? Is my electronic version different from the hard copy we received, Ms. Harbour?

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Your Honours, are you looking at the electronic version in e-court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes -- in e-court, no. I'm looking at the electronic version as was provided to the Chamber as an annex to the motion.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: I sent an e-mail on -- last Friday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: -- noting that there had been -- we -- we noticed that the previous version -- there was some formatting issues and lines and names had been shifted, so sometimes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then I'll check that. But could someone assist me in getting the right -- for 1992, 1994, the chart would have e-court exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: It's exhibit number P451. And 1994 to 1995 is the second page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I will ask Ms. Stewart to send the PDFs of these charts to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'll have a look at them. Thank you. You may proceed, meanwhile.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us now focus on the documents shown to you yesterday by the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we first have in e-court P457.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: By reading and discussing this document, you spoke about the procurement of ammunition by the 1st SMBR, as it says here. And this obviously refers to a brigade. And the request for ammunition is sent to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This appears to be a combat report dated 14th of May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In this chain, is it possible that the Main Staff could feature? Or perhaps you -- you did not address that issue at all.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can tell from this document, the Main Staff are not involved in this document. It's a document -- yes, it's a document from -- from the brigade to -- to the corps. Not involving the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now we need P458, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is, again, the -- a document produced by the SRK command.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And can we please look first at the penultimate page and then the last page in English and the last page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the course of commenting this document, there was a dilemma that arose with respect to something that we see on the penultimate page in English, for example, concerning the Blazuj Brigade. Let's move now to the last page in the English. Now the dilemma created here was by the Trnovo Brigade. And the dilemma was why these brigades were relocated by the SRK, whether they were -- belonged to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now let's go back to page 1 in both versions. And we need item 3. It's at the bottom of the page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This paragraph shows that involved in the action were parts of Herzegovina Corps and the Eastern Bosnia Corps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In detail now that we can read this page, we see the explanation of why the Trnovo Brigade is mentioned on the distribution list and so that explains that the Trnovo -- Trnovo Brigade looks very much from this possibly to be part of the Herzegovina Corps. That would be an example of an unconfirmed dotted line to the Herzegovina Corps for the Trnovo Brigade. But in a sense that's why the Trnovo Brigade doesn't appear in any of my charts.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we -- could we read the whole of paragraph 3, so next page. You -- meanwhile, please proceed, Mr. Lukic. At the same time, would this be a suitable time for a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would this be a good time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think it would be. We take a break. But could the witness first be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break and will resume at 10 minutes to 11.00

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Philipps, we're not going to go on for very long. We're just going to go through the documents that the Prosecutor showed you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please have in e-court P460. We're interested in paragraph 2 and 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is a document of the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps dated the 12th of September, 1992, when it was headed by Stanislav Galic. In paragraph 2, we see that Stanislav Galic insists that there should be consolidation and command and control at all levels and that all forces within the corps should be completely linked up. As you reviewed documents from the previous period, did you get the impression that, in the previous period, this had not been carried out; that is to say, consolidation and the establishment of command and control at all levels?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document was produced just after the meeting at Jahorina and General Galic had just taken over command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, and it's the type of document that is frequently produced and a senior officer when taking over an organisation; that is, he's trying to establish the way he means to go on, the way he intends to command the organisation. Frequently officers will make comments such as -- such as that. And at an earlier line says, stop the weekend war and the habits connected with it. What he is trying to do is improve the morale, the organisation, and the training of the organisation. That is a common type of document when a commander takes over. It's not necessarily a criticism of the previous command. If we look at the history of the formation of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, it would hardly be surprising that in the months from May through to September they were trying to put a corps together at the same time as fighting, so that's a very difficult thing to do, to bring an organisation together at the same time as fighting a battle. And that, the seeking to establish command and control, continued throughout the period from May to September and then onwards from September all the way through until the final -- until the end of the conflict. There was -- there was a continual effort by the commanders to gain and improve command and control throughout the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 3, we see that absolute agreement and unity with the civilian authorities and MUP forces at all levels is asked for and that no paramilitary units should be created. In your work, did you deal with the consequences because of the disagreements -- or, rather, the consequences of the disagreements with the civilian authorities and the MUP?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. My remit, really, has been to put together the structure of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps so that we can understand the command and control and the passage of information. But the political structures and the political intrigues do not form part of my chart.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know what was in the hands of civilians and that had to do with the military, including the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps? Did you study that? Did you study the supply channels that were in place? Did you include in your research the ministries of defence? And did you study how crimes were prosecuted, or rather, did you study the military judiciary? And did you know in whose hands military courts were?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Multiple questions there. No appears to be the answer to all those. I came across information relating to these things, which I read, and so I have some knowledge of them, but they did not form part of my report, and I haven't written reports on that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the documents that you reviewed, did you find any reference to paramilitaries in the territory that was covered by the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps? And what was the attitude of the command of this corps vis-a-vis the possible existence of such paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we can see from paragraph 3 of the document that you've shown me, which is that the theory put forward each time by the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps is that they did not want paramilitary organisations within their area. Paramilitary, by its definition, is outside their control. Military units, such as the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, need to control the military activity within that area, and so paramilitary was not a helpful organisation to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please have a look at P461.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In this document of the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, there are references to a meeting that should be attended by military and civilian representatives. I'm just going to ask you this: Was this something unusual, that is to say, for military and civilian representatives to meet? Does this kind of thing happen in other countries as well?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only speak from the point of view of the British Army, where it would be very rare for politicians to be involved in a meeting where military decisions are to be made, except at the very highest level. At corps level, at brigade level, it would be unheard of, if you like, for politicians to be involved in military decisions. Politicians are involved in establishing the aim of a military operation, but then the actual activity is entirely down to the military commanders. So, for me, this is an interesting example of relatively low-level military commanders being involved with the political leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If supplies for the military were in the hands of civilian organs, and if you were to know that, would you still find if strange or unusual?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's fair to say that the set of circumstances surrounding this meeting are strange and unusual. A civil war, or whatever we want to call this war, is -- it's not a normal set of military operations. It is out of the ordinary. And so events like this, which are out of the ordinary, seem to occur often. And the production of supplies, clearly, in any military context, is in the hands of civilian factories.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In relation to this, we are now going to look at document P462. We just need the first page. The department for security-intelligence affairs of the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps compiled an Official Note on the 4th of August, 1995. It is evident from the document that the corps commander is being criticised for carrying out personnel changes in accordance with the wishes of the SDS, that is to say, political wishes, rather than in accordance with the military values upheld by a military commander. Did you come across that? This is probably one of the documents that you had been shown. Namely, that military commanders were appointed in accordance with the wishes of those outside the military and under pressure that they brought to bear?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- concluding that such an event took place from one document that we have in front of us is a dangerous step. This is a document written by a junior officer about a senior officer. It is -- it is rare for a subordinate to write such a document about his commanding officer, about his commander. It would be a -- a shocking thing for an officer to do and to make it an Official Note, in such a way. If we take the contents to be true - and that's an if - then it would be a -- a very poor thing for an officer to make appointments based on political decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You say a junior officer criticizing a senior officer. You studied the system of command and control of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. Isn't it a fact that the security organ, the organ for security and intelligence as it was called, and this is actually an officer who holds a junior rank, in actual fact?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think if we go to the signature page, is it a Bukva --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- the surname of the officer? And he has criticised the corps commander. Was he a major, Bukva? That's from memory. If we could see the next page we could further --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yeah, it is. Yeah, we can see the -- you are right. He is. My question is whether it is always the situation that the officer of a security organ is younger than the commander of the corps.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I -- by junior I meant in rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In rank?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. I'm -- I think the rank as well.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's -- it would be unusual if the -- the officer in charge of intelligence and security were a higher rank than the corps commander. I've never known such an event.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Exactly. So this is normal situation, actually, that he has to criticise somebody who is above him, because it's his job.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: My criticism is the method and the way that it is done. If he had felt such a thing were occurring, it would be very strange to put it into an Official Note. But we don't know the history. We don't know what -- he may have tried to do this verbally. There's all sorts of history. But to put it into an Official Note, to make it official, is a very serious matter in this case. It would be rare for an officer to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In paragraph 4, this officer also says: "[In English]: "Therefore" -- it's in the middle of paragraph. "Therefore, the current situation speaks of the SRK artillery being under the party's direct supervision." [Interpretation] During the course of your work, did you come across anything like that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is -- this is the only document I've seen suggesting that the artillery might be under a form of political control because the officers in charge of that artillery were members of a party.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please have in e-court, P463.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You commented upon paragraph 6.2, I think, from this document. Artillery support.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We saw this document yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mm-hm. I would kindly ask that we now take a look at paragraph 1, where it says: "An attack is expected by enemy forces, the strength of a corps (Sarajevo), and by Tactical Group 2, Tactical Group 1, four independent brigades, approximately, several detachments, and numerous special and other units." Further down, there is an assessment or, rather, an estimate of the number of people who will be involved in these operations from the enemy side. If we add all of that up, we see that an attack is being expected from three sides of over 40.000 armed men. Is it customary in such situations to ask for artillery support? What is your opinion?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, clearly, in such an event the only means of stopping such an attack would very possibly be the use of artillery and mortars and small arms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, could you make me the calculation for the 40.000?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mm-hm. On the first page we have only for the first BiH army corps 35.000 people, and 3.000 people as special units in the second paragraph. Then third paragraph he's talking about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me see. Total strength of the forces in Sarajevo is estimate at about 35.000. You mean they would all be -- you understand them all to be included.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then we have separately, Tactical Group 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. If you include the 35.000 --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's the estimate. Probably their estimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, what the strength of the forces. Yes. I was just wondering whether --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: From the point 1 it says that they expect that the whole corps would attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now I see it. Thank you. You have clarified the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now, at the end, let us look at document -- let me first find it because it was not admitted. And it can be located by ERN number, which is 0529248.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's 65 ter 28501.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I suppose you have seen this document because the Prosecution tendered it into evidence through you. This is a document from the command of the SRK dated the 4th of January, 1995, and that's the minutes of the meeting of commanders of brigades, regiments, and independent battalions. I'm not going to read all of it. On page 2, and it starts on page 1 in B/C/S, and page 2 in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Harbour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: I only rise to clarify that the Prosecution did not tender this document through this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that was already indicated by Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed. You meanwhile re-read -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On page 2 of the English, we can see that it reads [In English] Stojanovic is speaking. [Interpretation] He is speaking, and I'm going to paraphrase this in order to save time. He says that the soldiers were not insufficiently trained - it's somewhere in the middle - for the use of equipment in shifts. [In English] Insufficient training of commanders, platoon commanders, in detachments and platoons. The brigade command is manned up to 30 per cent of its capacity. [Interpretation] Did you know, as far as the beginning of 1995, which is the last year of war, that the problem of the lack of training still existed among the troops, including platoon commanders, et cetera. Were you aware of the fact that the troops of the SRK were actually poorly trained soldiers?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's fair to say they were relatively poorly trained. But what is interesting is throughout the period of 1992 to 1995, the commanders were striving to train and improve the training of those soldiers and that training is part of the life of a soldier. When you are not doing active service, you're training. And if you're not getting fit in some way, you're training. And most soldiers will tell you that they spend all their time training. And that is reflected, I think, in these documents. Having said that, of course, the level of training is another matter, and most posts in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, the posts for commanders, were filled by officers who were junior in rank than that actually required to fulfil the post. But, nevertheless, this is a good example of the amount of work put in by the corps command and by the brigade commanders to improve the training of the troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you also aware of the information that the brigade command and how widespread that was in the SRK and that they were only manned up to 30 per cent of its capacity and what were the effects of that fact on the troops?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was clearly a shortage of senior officers and of trained staff officers, not only at brigade level but at corps level. The effect of that would be a breakdown in communication, a breakdown in supply, and a breakdown in the command and control at some points of soldiers and troops under command. But there were certain aspects of this warfare that meant certain specialist officers were not required, fewer were required. But nevertheless, 30 per cent is a low number to have in a brigade headquarters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Part of the question also was - but it was a bit of a composite question - how widespread that was in the SRK. So apart from the specific brigade discussed here, do you have any knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think, really, at brigade command level and at corps command level they were all undermanned. There were fewer officers than would be required normally for a full command structure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But for the specific brigade the number of 30 per cent is mentioned. Could you confirm that for the others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would have to look at the figures for the others, but I would not be surprised if they were half or less of the number of officers normally expected in a headquarters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Also towards the end of this paragraph: A proposal is made: [In English] "I propose" -- It's the last sentence, actually. "I propose that MUP should be under army's command in the defence areas where it is engaged at." [Interpretation] Did you come across information that you included that MUP forces were not resubordinated to the VRS even when they were engaged in combat operations?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As my chart shows, I have no MUP shown as being directly under the chart -- under the command of the -- the corps. Occasionally MUP forces were used in specific operations where they might be placed under temporary command. I think an example would be Lukavac 93, an operation south of Sarajevo, where a MUP battalion was placed under the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps for a temporary period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Towards the bottom of the page, there's the speech by Lieutenant-Colonel Milorad Sehovac, and he says that the average age of his troops is over 50. Did you have an opportunity to confirm this through your research, that the age range was as indicated here? Maybe not in all units, but in some, nevertheless.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have certainly seen some combat reports where the entire age range of a brigade would be broken down into percentages and numbers so that one can see that the average age of a brigade and the age of the soldiers was generally higher than that expected in combat units. So people are not 18, 19, and 20, as modern soldiers often are, but in this conflict they were frequently over 30 and sometimes over 50. There are advantages and disadvantages in such a situation. In a static warfare situation, if we look at the average age of soldiers -- for example, in the First World War, they were much older, and older soldiers can be wiser soldiers, but they do not have the fitness or the fighting capability of younger soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On the next page, page 3 of the English version, we can see that this commander, as well, is complaining - and you can find it in line 4 from the top: "[In English] ... brigade is meant with officers only 30 per cent of its capacity."

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So as you said yourself, there were such instances in other brigades as well, that is to say that the level of manning was up to 30, but in this same document we can see instances where the level of manning was 70 per cent. Then on page 7 there's reference to the level of manning of troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have page 7 in English. The timeline is 1245. This is a contribution by Captain Petrusic. And then in line 3, it is said --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would Mr. Lukic kindly provide a reference in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you're invited to provide a reference in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In B/C/S, we can find this on page 5 at the very top. It's 1246 hours, although in English it says 1245. But I don't see that as a major mistake. And this commander also says that in his unit the average age is between 42 and 45 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now my question is: Was it also the case that the level of manning, in terms of regular soldiers, was below the requirement.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The level of manning of -- in this case anti-tank batteries, is here listed as -- as 40 per cent of the complement. However, one has to remember that a regular anti-tank battery will be moving from place to place, almost continuously, in order to -- to fight, whereas this mixed anti-armoured artillery regiment was mainly static. And although 40 per cent is only just enough people to fight with, it is nevertheless sufficient to fight a battery with such reduced numbers provided it is not moving continuously in the battle-field. So reduction in numbers in the artillery is less serious in some respects because of the nature of this warfare than it would have been in the infantry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: And would you like me to comment on the average age? The average age of artillery soldiers is generally higher, much higher, than infantry soldiers due to the level of training required. That's certainly the case in the British Army. Whether it is the case in the SRK -- it appears that they are older in this case. 42 to 45 is a high average age for artillery. There is a lot of physical work involved. And as people get older they're less capable of performing the very physical work of moving shells.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to read only one portion of this document because I'm not sure that the translation is correct that we have on the screen, so I'm going to read it in B/C/S. "1410 hours, Lieutenant-Colonel Petar Tomic addressed the General and pointed out to the fact that there is incorrect reporting coming from your" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, we don't have it on the screen. We don't have it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't want to have it on the screen. I want translation first. So the translators can translate what I'm reading from the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But it's helpful for them to see it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If you want it that way, Your Honour, then it's page 10 of English version and page 6 of B/C/S version. The hour is 1410. I will read again: [Interpretation] "1410 hours, Lieutenant-Colonel Petar Tomic addressed the General and indicated that the units are providing incorrect reports ..." I thank the interpreters. Because in the English translation, we see the word "irregular" [in English] and that's exactly the difference we wanted to point out.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Philipps, in your work did you have an occasion to check to what extent the reporting, which is something that is conducted along the chain of command upwards, was correct and how consistent it was with what was actually happening on the ground? Did you deal with these issues at all?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would Mr. Lukic kindly switch off his microphone when not using it, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm to some extent guilty of having my microphone now and then open when it should be closed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, when I looked at the reports from units of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, one of the methods of establishing that such a report is real, that is, it's not a forgery or it's not a later production, is to compare the events mentioned in the report with occurrences; that is, where weather events are described such as fog, and one can check whether it was foggy on that day; where events such as shelling incidents occur, one can compare that with other reports to see whether such a shelling incident occurred. So that was done really from point of view to check the authenticity of the document. They had stamps. They were typed correctly. They had signatures. But also they matched the events that were occurring in Sarajevo which convinced me of their authenticity. Furthermore, the reports were of different quality, so rather, as Petar Tomic says, they did not always follow the correct format. Most of them followed the correct format in requesting ammunition at the right place, explaining what the enemy was doing, but many would be rambling, some would be confused and be difficult for the staff to extract the data that they required. So the reports reflected the capabilities of the officers that were writing them. Some were professional and some were written by individuals who were in a rank or in a position that was higher than their true capability.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it true that, at the very top level of the corps, and especially in lower-ranking units, there were quite a few reserve officers?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think many of the posts were -- were manned by reserve officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Philipps, thank you. This is all I had, as regards the questions that I had for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I would like to tender into evidence in this case the document that we have just looked at, 65 ter 28501.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 28501 becomes Exhibit D94, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that from the other exhibits, just as the Galic transcript, that you have quoted to the relevant portion and you do not need them to be admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, you are right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Harbour, I'm looking at the clock. We'll take a break -- we would normally take a break in approximately five minutes from now. How much time would you need for re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Perhaps 20 minutes to half an hour, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I think it would be wiser to take the break first. Could Mr. Philipps be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: With your leave, would be it possible if General Mladic stays in the courtroom and inspect the maps while we're on the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There's no problem with that. Then I take it that the curtains will be down anyhow so that the courtroom is a private place and the audience not to be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take a break, and we'll resume at ten minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Harbour, if you are ready, you may re-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Mr. Philipps, yesterday, at transcript page 4717, Mr. Lukic asked you a question about two units that did not exist simultaneously but both of which appear on your chart. You responded, and I quote: "That is correct. Because the chart covers a period of time, it shows the passage of one unit to another, in the same way it shows two corps commanders in the corps headquarters when, of course, there was only ever corps commander at any one time." Can you please explain what you meant when you said "there can only be one corps commander at any one time"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Any military organisation has a commander, and there can only ever be one commander of a military organisation. My chart simply shows the passage of command and control from one commander to another, and that's why two are shown on the chart. There can only ever be one commander of an organisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Is there any name for this principle that you've described whereby there can only be one commander at a time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You hear various phrase used, singularity of command and such phrase. So it's the fact that only one person can be in charge.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: As far as you know, from reviewing VRS materials, was this principle followed by the SRK throughout the period covered by your charts?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The SRK used JNA principles and JNA methodology and that requires the -- the singularity of command; that is, one commander in charge of an organisation with deputies and assistants, but he himself is the only person that is required to make the decisions.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Again, from your analysis, was this principle followed by the VRS as a whole and by General Mladic during that period?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know it would very unusual for that to be not the case. So as far I know, the whole of the VRS would have followed the same JNA principles of one person in charge of an organisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: We've discussed exhibit number P458, which is a SRK order dated 7 June 1992. At the temporary transcript pages 22 to 23 today, in reference to this exhibit, you mentioned that: "This -- the explanation of why the Trnovo Brigade is mentioned on the distribution list."

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Could we please have 65 ter 3710 on the screen. What will appear is a 6 June 1992 directive of the then-Lieutenant-General Mladic of the VRS Main Staff. If we could turn to page 4 of the English, and I apologise, I don't have the reference for the B/C/S, but we're interested in the Herzegovina Corps, it's the very last paragraph of the English version. The very last sentence says: "Form a strong tactical group in order to prevent the breakthrough of the enemy from Ivan Sedlo and Konjic towards Kalinovik and Trnovo using a portion of force co-acting with Sarajevo-Romanija Corps to deblock the communication Sarajevo-Trnovo." As we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is page 3 in the B/C/S. I think it's -- yes. We have it already, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But we need the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: If we could please turn to the following page in English to complete the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: As we saw in P458, the Trnovo Brigade was a recipient of an order from the SRK command, the SRK commander, the next day. What does this indicate about command and control from Mladic in the VRS to the corps level and to the brigade level?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- this order shows the formation, interestingly enough, again of a tactical group for a specific purpose. So we see again a temporary tactical group being formed by the order of General Mladic, and he's using a brigade from another corps, from the Herzegovina Corps, based on Trnovo, that is the Trnovo brigade, and this brigade is being put at the disposal of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps as a tactical group to -- along with other troops to enable a specific purpose to be fulfilled. And we see from this that really the VRS, particularly General Mladic, has the ability to -- to reassign and -- and organise the corps in such a way that they can redistribute troops from one corps to another for a temporary purpose.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Could I tender this into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 3710 becomes Exhibit P474, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: At temporary transcript page 10 today, Mr. Lukic asked you the following question: --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, is the B/C/S complete? I'm looking at page 3. In English it ends with Commander Lieutenant-General Ratko Mladic, and then to who it was sent -- oh, there we have it. Yes. Yes, thank you. Well, it's not complete to the extent that the last portion, apparently, is missing there. The last line where, of course, it would be interesting to see whether it was also sent to the Trnovo Brigade. But if you would have a better copy then that would be appreciated. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we will look for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so. And meanwhile continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: At page 10 today, the question was put to you: "Do you remember that you mentioned that platoon Vasko's Battalion and that you determined that it was a paramilitary formation?" In the Galic case, I'd like to read a portion of your testimony from that case to you. On the 10th of July, 2002, at transcript page T-11564, while discussing the VP numbers of the Vasko and other platoons and units, you said: "The fact that any of these units, including Vasko's Platoon, have a VP number, 7491, shows them to be part of the organisation of the Ilijas Brigade and, in addition, the number 20 indicates it to be a separate unit of the Ilijas Brigade." You then pointed out that "there are several, several documents referring to that platoon." In light of that prior testimony, would you agree with Mr. Lukic's characterisation of your prior testimony in court today?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If by that you mean that Mr. Lukic suggested that I called Vasko's Platoon a paramilitary formation, then I have not called Vasko's Platoon a paramilitary formation because it has a VP number. And I'm -- by my prior testimony in Galic, I hope it's clear that it's not a paramilitary organisation and is part of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: At transcript page 4729 yesterday, you were asked if the Main Staff had artillery weapons. And today, at transcript page 21 to 22, regarding Exhibit P457, which is a report by the 1st SMBR to the SRK, in which the brigade requested ammunition, Mr. Lukic asked you: "In this chain, is it possible that the Main Staff could feature? Or perhaps you -- you did not address that issue at all." And you did respond that as far as you could tell from the document, the Main Staff were not involved in that document. I would like to look at exhibit -- or 65 ter number 12103. This is from the SRK command to the command of the Ilidza Brigade. The first sentence says that a 128-millimetre Oganj VBR was in that unit's possession. The next sentence states that this weapon could not be used effectively in the Ilidza Brigade's area, so the corps command had informed the Main Staff of the VRS. In the next paragraph, we see that the Main Staff ordered the Ilidza Brigade to immediately return this multiple rocket-launcher to the 4th map unit of the SRK. Then we read that the Main Staff would inform the Drina Corps, from which the weapon came to the Ilidza Brigade, that it would be placed at the disposal of the SRK. What does this document indicate about the VRS commander's ability to control ammunition and weapons?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we should understand that the Main Staff itself did not have its own artillery. It did not have artillery units directly attached to it. The artillery that it was able to use were attached and part of corps units. So the corps controlled the artillery either in artillery regiments or they passed that artillery down to the brigades, to the brigade commanders to have command of. But the VRS retained the ability to redistribute that artillery between brigades and to different corps depending on the military situation. This is an example of the Chief of Staff of the Main Staff ensuring that a rocket-launcher that is in a particular unit of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps is returned back to the mixed artillery regiment so that it can be used. So it's an example of the chain of command: The VRS passing an order through the corps commander and the corps command passing that down to the brigade commander so that the artillery is in an appropriate position for it to be used for the military purpose.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: As you just stated, the VRS retained the ability to re-direct the artillery between brigade and to different corps, and in light of your recent comments about singularity of command: When you refer to the VRS is that -- can you be more specific?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this case it actually mentions the Chief of Staff of the Main Staff. He would have been directed by the commander of the VRS, Main Staff, that is, General Mladic, for any particular action. The Chief of Staff was merely fulfilling the orders of the general in charge.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
